passage:
The school counsellor's room smelled of crayons. Omkar and Shalini sat on two tiny chairs while their son Aarush, six, played with blocks in the corner.

It had started at pickup. Aarush wanted the tablet; Omkar said "No, never on school days"; Shalini said "Fine, twenty minutes." Then they argued, right there at the gate, while Aarush looked from one to the other.

"He's started asking me first for everything," Omkar admitted. "Because I'm the fun one," Shalini said, then winced. "That's not great either, is it?"

The counsellor, Mrs. Dsouza, asked them to choose only three shared rules and to decide them away from Aarush. They agreed: tablet only on weekends, bedtime at eight-thirty, and any "no" from one parent is a "no" from both.

"And if we disagree?" Omkar asked.

"Then you say, 'We'll talk and tell you,' and you talk later."

In the corner, Aarush's tower was getting very tall.

qa.q: What were the three shared rules Omkar and Shalini agreed on?
qa.a: Tablet only on weekends, bedtime at eight-thirty, and any "no" from one parent is a "no" from both.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when she called herself "the fun one"?
qa.a: Shalini felt uneasy and a little ashamed, wincing as she realised that role wasn't good either.

qa.q: Why was it wise to set the rules away from Aarush?
qa.a: Agreeing privately let the parents back each other up in front of him, instead of arguing and splitting into a harsh parent and a fun parent.

qa.q: How might Aarush have felt during the argument at the gate?
qa.a: Aarush probably felt confused and uneasy, looking from one parent to the other.

grounding: The passage shows parents who disagree on discipline and argue in front of their child, who agree privately on a few shared rules and back each other up.

passage:
Imtiaz,

I'm writing this after the kids are asleep because I don't want to argue again in front of them.

Tonight, when Zayan wouldn't eat his vegetables, I said he'd get no dessert, and you slipped him a chocolate under the table and winked. He saw me see it. I felt so small, and so angry, that I left the room.

This keeps happening. I've become the strict one and you're the fun one. I don't want that. I don't want our kids to learn that if Ammi says no, they go to Abbu.

My friend Sonali said something that stuck: "Pick three rules together and never break them in front of the kids." So here are mine: food first, then sweets; screens off at eight; no hitting, ever. What are yours?

If you disagree with me in the moment, say "We'll talk later." I'll do the same for you.

Can we talk on Saturday, just us?

Rehana

qa.q: What did Imtiaz slip Zayan under the table?
qa.a: He slipped Zayan a chocolate.

qa.q: What did Rehana feel when Imtiaz winked and gave Zayan the chocolate?
qa.a: Rehana felt small and angry, undermined in front of their son.

qa.q: What does Rehana suggest so they stop undermining each other?
qa.a: Agreeing on three shared rules privately, backing each other in front of the children, and saying "We'll talk later" when they disagree.

qa.q: How might Imtiaz see his wink at the table?
qa.a: Imtiaz may have seen it as harmless fun, not realising it made Rehana the harsh one.

grounding: A letter shows a mother whose husband undermines her discipline in front of their child, asking to agree privately on a few rules and back each other publicly.

passage:
Pradeep, you think you are the first parent to miss things for work? Sit down. Your Vasudha paati was a doctor, remember.

When your mother was small, I did night duty at the government hospital three times a week. I missed her first steps. I missed her school play; she was a tree. I would come home at seven in the morning and she'd be asleep, and I would stand at her bed feeling like a thief who had stolen her own child's days.

For two years I lived in that guilt, and it made me snappy and tired on the days I was home.

Then I made two promises. Every Sunday breakfast was ours, dosas and no hospital calls. And on nights off, I read to her, one chapter, no matter how tired. That's all.

You can't be everywhere, kanna. Be completely there when you are. And forgive yourself for the rest.

qa.q: What part did Pradeep's mother play in the school play?
qa.a: She was a tree.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel standing at her daughter's bed after night duty?
qa.a: She felt guilty, like a thief who had stolen her own child's days.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vasudha's story?
qa.a: She chose two protected times, Sunday breakfasts and bedtime reading on nights off, and gave them her full attention.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's daughter have felt about the Sunday dosas?
qa.a: She probably felt loved and looked forward to them, knowing her mother was fully hers then.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young mother working long hours and guilty about missing her child's moments, who chooses protected times of full attention and forgives herself.

passage:
The flight from Hyderabad was delayed by three hours, and Sumit sat at the gate watching the minutes of Lokesh's annual day go by on his phone. His son, five, was a sunflower. Sumit had promised.

He felt sick. This was the third event this year. He ran a small logistics firm, and when a truck broke down, the phone didn't care who was dancing.

His wife sent a video: Lokesh on stage, searching the crowd, then waving at her. Sumit watched it four times.

He landed at eleven. Lokesh was asleep. Sumit sat on the bed in the dark.

The next morning he made two decisions and wrote them on the fridge whiteboard. Every Sunday morning: cycling with Papa, phone in the drawer. Every Wednesday: Papa does bedtime.

"Sorry I missed it, beta. Show me your sunflower dance?" Lokesh danced it in the kitchen, twice, in his pyjamas. Sumit clapped like the whole audience.

qa.q: What was Lokesh at the annual day?
qa.a: He was a sunflower.

passage:
At the community centre in Vijayawada, Leela taught the Tuesday tailoring class, and on school holidays Vandana, five, came along. She sat at the small table with scraps and a blunt needle and copied everything: how Leela licked the thread, how she pushed her glasses up, how she said "Very good, very good" to each student.

It made Leela's heart warm. It also made her careful. Every move was being learned.

That Tuesday a student ruined a blouse, and Leela snapped, "How many times must I tell you?" The room went quiet. Vandana stared at her with big eyes.

Leela's stomach dropped. She took a breath, went to the student and said, "I'm sorry, I spoke rudely. Let's unpick it together." The student smiled shakily.

On the bus home, Vandana said, "Amma, you said sorry to the big girl." "Yes. When I'm wrong, I say sorry." Vandana nodded seriously, as if filing it away.

qa.a: She copied how Leela licked the thread, pushed her glasses up and said "Very good, very good" to each student.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Vandana stared at her after she snapped?
qa.a: Leela felt her stomach drop with shame, aware that her daughter was learning from everything she did.

qa.a: The student probably felt relieved and respected, smiling shakily as they fixed the blouse together.

passage:
Dear Jaya,

You are four, and you can't read this yet. I'm writing it for when you can.

This week you put on my spectacles, held a newspaper upside down and said, "I'm Papa. I'm very busy." Yesterday you told the vegetable seller that your father can lift a car. You look at me as if I'm a superhero. It fills my chest. It also scares me, because I'm not.

On Sunday I shouted at an auto driver who cut us off. You were in the back seat. Afterwards you shouted "Idiot!" at your doll. My face went hot. So I went back to the auto stand on Monday, with you, and I said sorry to that driver. You watched the whole thing.

One day you'll see I'm just a man who gets angry and makes mistakes. I hope you'll also remember that I said sorry, and that I loved you the whole time.

Your Papa, Ojas

passage:
At one in the morning, in his Gachibowli flat, Tushar was still scrolling. College photos from eight years ago: the hostel roof, Wasim's terrible moustache, the four of them squeezed on one scooter at the lake. He could almost hear Wasim's laugh.

Now Wasim had twins and a job in Pune. They hadn't spoken since his wedding. Tushar felt a slow ache under his ribs. Where had all that closeness gone?

He started typing: "Why don't you ever call?" Then deleted it.

He sent the moustache photo instead. "Found this. Still the worst decision of your life. Miss you, yaar."

In the morning there was a reply. "HAHA burn it. Miss you too. Twins have destroyed me."

Tushar grinned. "I'm in Pune on the 14th for work. Chai for twenty minutes?" "Done."

It wouldn't be the hostel roof. It would be twenty minutes, probably with a baby crying. That was fine.

qa.q: Where did Wasim now work?
qa.a: Wasim now had a job in Pune.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he scrolled the old photos?
qa.a: Tushar felt nostalgic and a slow ache of missing Wasim and their old closeness.

qa.q: Why was the message Tushar sent better than the first one he typed?
qa.a: It was warm and light instead of blaming, and it opened the door to a small, realistic plan for chai.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel receiving the photo?
qa.a: Wasim likely felt amused and touched, replying that he missed Tushar too 🙂

"Rukku? It's Manjula. Is this a bad time?"

"Manju! No, no. I'm just stirring the sambar with a baby on my hip. Talk."

"I was going through the old photos. Remember the rain at Lalbagh, when we missed the last bus?"

"And walked home singing? My mother nearly killed me." Rukmini laughed. "God, I miss that."

"Me too. I miss you. I keep thinking we should go back to how it was. Every weekend together."

A pause. "Manju... I can't do every weekend now. With the baby and Ravi's shifts, I barely see my own face."

Manjula felt a small sting, then let it go. "Okay. What about a call on the first Sunday of every month? Twenty minutes. Sambar optional."

"Yes. That I can do. And when she's older, Lalbagh. In the rain."

"Deal."

Manjula hung up smiling, a little wistful. It wasn't the old friendship. It was still theirs.

passage:
You asked how my year's been. I'm Imran. Mostly fine. But there's one thing I keep chewing on.

Usha and I were friends since school. Daily voice notes, the kind of friend who knew my blood group and my worst poem. In March she just stopped replying. Blue ticks, no answer. Then not even blue ticks.

For weeks I felt dropped and confused. I went over every conversation. Had I said something? Was she ever really my friend?

Then I did one thing. I wrote: "Usha, I miss you. If something's wrong, or if I did something, I'd like to know. If you need space, that's okay too." No blame. And I sent it once.

She hasn't replied. It's been four months.

And I've decided not to rewrite fifteen years as fake. Those voice notes were real. Maybe her life is hard right now. Maybe she's done. Either way, what we had was real.

qa.q: When did Usha stop replying?
qa.a: She stopped replying in March.

qa.q: How did Imran feel in the weeks after Usha went silent?
qa.a: Imran felt dropped and confused, going over every conversation and doubting the friendship.

qa.q: What made Imran's single message a wise step?
qa.a: It reached out directly without blame, left room for her to need space, and Imran accepted the silence without chasing her.

qa.q: How might Usha be seeing things during her silence?
qa.a: We can't know; she may be struggling with something hard, or she may have moved on, which is why Imran avoids assuming the worst.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone whose close friend has stopped replying, who reaches out once without blame, accepts silence and does not rewrite the friendship as fake.

passage:
First Monday. Hafsa noticed Yash hadn't answered in nine days, not even to the meme about their old professor. They used to talk every evening. She felt a sharp, stupid hurt. Had he found better friends at his new job?

The next Saturday. After a week of drafting angry versions, she sent one calm message: "Hey, I've missed you. Are you okay? If I've upset you, tell me. No pressure either way." Then she put the phone in a drawer and went for a long walk, trying not to check it.

Two weeks later. Yash replied late at night. "Sorry. I lost the job in October and haven't told anyone. I've been hiding from everyone, not just you."

Hafsa read it twice, her throat tight. The story she'd told herself, that he'd dropped her, had been wrong. "Thank you for telling me. Want to get chai on Sunday? We don't have to talk about work." He sent a thumbs-up. It was a start.

qa.q: How many days had Yash not answered when Hafsa first noticed?
qa.a: He hadn't answered in nine days.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a sharp hurt, puzzled and afraid Yash had found better friends.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do well in reaching out?
qa.a: She sent one calm, direct message without blame, gave him space, and accepted his answer with warmth.

qa.q: How was Yash experiencing those weeks of silence?
qa.a: Yash was ashamed and hiding after losing his job, pulling away from everyone, not just Hafsa.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose close friend stopped replying, who reaches out once without blame and accepts the answer rather than rewriting the friendship.

passage:
Every Pongal, Shalini went home to her village near Thanjavur, and every year she avoided the lane where Vasudha lived. Vasudha had written to her, called her, even sent a wedding card three years ago. Shalini, buried in her Chennai job and her own marriage, had never gone. She'd sent nothing, not even a message.

This year, buying jaggery at the corner shop, she turned and there was Vasudha, holding a toddler on her hip.

Shalini's face went hot. A dozen excuses rose: the office, the traffic, the in-laws. She swallowed them.

"Vasu. I've missed you. I'm sorry I disappeared. I have no good reason."

Vasudha looked at her for a long moment. "I stopped expecting you." Then her face softened slightly. "This is Kavin."

Shalini knelt and shook the boy's fat hand. That night she sent Vasudha a photo of the kolam she'd drawn. The next Sunday, from Chennai, she sent another.

qa.q: What was Shalini buying at the corner shop?
qa.a: She was buying jaggery.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when she saw Vasudha?
qa.a: Shalini felt guilty and embarrassed, her face hot, with many excuses rising up.

qa.q: Why was Shalini's short apology the right choice?

qa.q: How does Vasudha feel meeting Shalini again?
qa.a: Vasudha feels hurt and guarded, having stopped expecting her, but she softens a little by introducing her son.

At the Dussehra fair in Sirsa, Neelam saw Kashish before Kashish saw her, and ducked behind the bangle stall.

Kashish had cleared the state service exam in June. Her photo had been in the local paper. Her father had distributed laddoos to the whole mohalla. Neelam had failed the same exam twice. She hadn't called Kashish once since the result.

Standing behind the bangles, Neelam felt jealousy burn in her throat, and under it something sadder. She wanted it too. Not Kashish's life. Her own chance.

That was useful to know. It meant she should sit the exam once more, and maybe ask Kashish how she'd prepared.

She stepped out. "Kashish!" Kashish turned, her face lighting up, then uncertain.

"Congratulations. Really. I should have called. I was jealous and I'm sorry."

Kashish hugged her, bangles clinking. "I missed you so much. Come for tea tomorrow. I'll give you all my notes."

passage:
At the insurance office in Kochi, Joseph's new nameplate said Team Lead. Vikas, who had joined the same week three years ago, now sat two desks away and barely said good morning.

In the pantry, Joseph tried. "Chai?" "I'm fine." Vikas left with his bottle.

Joseph felt awkward and oddly lonely. He hadn't changed. But he could see how the nameplate looked from Vikas's chair.

That Friday he didn't mention the promotion or the new targets. He found Vikas at the bike stand. "How's your mother's knee after the surgery?"

Vikas blinked. "Better. She's walking to the church again."

"That's great. And your running? You were training for the half marathon."

"Still am. Twenty kilometres last Sunday."

"Madman," Joseph said. Vikas almost smiled. On Monday he said good morning first, and on Wednesday they had chai together, talking about anything but work.

passage:
Dear Ganga,

It's been two months since my wedding, and I've noticed you've gone quiet. You held my dupatta when I was a shaking bride, and then you left the reception early, and you haven't answered my last three messages. I might be wrong. But I think something changed between us, and I miss you.

I know my messages lately have been all about the wedding, the new house, Faraz's family. That must have been a lot to scroll through. I'm sorry if it felt like I was showing off. I wasn't trying to.

I want to hear about you. How is the job at the library? Did you ever finish that mural in your room? Is your mother still making those terrible experimental pickles?

Marriage hasn't replaced you. You were my first friend in this city, my sister in everything but blood, and you still are. You can tell me anything, including that you're annoyed with me.

Tea at our old place, Saturday at four?

Noor

passage:
I'm Zubin, and for two years I was the one who always called Sonali.

Her birthday: I called. Her promotion: I called. When her grandmother died, I drove to Nashik. She'd pick up sometimes, be lovely for ten minutes, and then nothing until I called again. I never got a call from her in those years except once, to borrow my car.

One night I scrolled back through my call log and felt foolish. Was I loyal or just a doormat?

I talked it over with my cousin, who said, "Don't punish her. Just stop carrying it all." So I tried an experiment. I stopped calling first. I kept replying warmly whenever she messaged.

It's been three months. She's called twice. Short calls, but hers. Our friendship is smaller than I wanted. But it's real, and I'm not angry about it. I'd rather have a true small friendship than a big one I hold up alone.

qa.q: What was the one time Sonali called Zubin during those years?
qa.a: She called once, to borrow Zubin's car.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel scrolling back through the call log?
qa.a: Zubin felt foolish and unsure, wondering whether the loyalty had turned into being a doormat.

qa.q: What did Zubin's experiment show?
qa.a: By stopping calling first while staying warm, Zubin could see how much effort was mutual and let the friendship settle at its natural level.

qa.q: How might Sonali see the change in Zubin?
qa.a: Sonali may have noticed the quiet and missed Zubin, since she began calling on her own.

grounding: A first-person account shows someone who keeps calling a friend who rarely calls back, who checks whether the effort is mutual and lets the friendship find its level without resentment.

passage:
Employee wellbeing counselling note, Thursday. Maria, 24, second session.

Maria spent most of the hour talking about her friend Manoj, who moved to Bengaluru last year. She calls him every Sunday; he answers about one in four times and rarely calls back. She showed me her phone: eleven outgoing calls in a row. She laughed, then said, "Am I an idiot for still trying?" Her voice wobbled.

I asked what she valued in the friendship. She said he had stayed with her in hospital when she had dengue, the whole week. Loyalty clearly matters a great deal to her, and she said she felt ashamed to want more back.

We talked about mutual effort. I suggested she stop keeping count and instead notice, over a month, whether any effort comes from him. She decided to send him one honest message: "I miss you. I'd love it if you called sometimes too."

Plan: review next Thursday.

qa.q: How many outgoing calls in a row were on Maria's phone?
qa.a: There were eleven outgoing calls in a row.

qa.q: How did Maria feel as she asked if she was an idiot for still trying?
qa.a: Maria felt foolish and ashamed, her voice wobbling, torn between loyalty and wanting more back.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest to Maria?
qa.a: To stop keeping count and watch over a month whether any effort comes from Manoj, and to tell him honestly she'd like him to call too.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the friendship now that he is in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Manoj may still care about Maria but be caught up in his new life, without realising how one-sided the calls have become.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman who keeps calling a friend who rarely calls back, checking whether effort is mutual and letting the friendship find its level.

Before. A Sunday in May. Manjula found the old train ticket in a book: Mysuru to Ooty, 2019, her and Pallavi. There had been no fight. Pallavi moved to Delhi, calls got shorter, then stopped. Manjula held the ticket and felt a grief so quiet she almost didn't recognise it. She told no one. Who mourns a friendship?

During. The next Thursday she let herself remember properly. She wrote a page in her notebook: Pallavi teaching her to swim at twenty-two, their night on the station bench, the way Pallavi always ordered for both of them. She cried a little. She stuck the ticket on the page.

After. Six weeks later, a colleague named Tanu asked her to join a pottery class. Manjula nearly said no. Tanu wasn't like Pallavi at all: quiet, precise, allergic to trains. She said yes anyway. At the second class Tanu made a lopsided cup and laughed until she snorted. Manjula laughed too.

qa.q: Where was the old train ticket from?
qa.a: It was a ticket from Mysuru to Ooty, from 2019.

qa.q: What did Manjula feel holding the old ticket?
qa.a: Manjula felt a quiet grief for the lost friendship, one she felt nobody else would acknowledge.

qa.q: How did Manjula care for her grief?
qa.a: She let herself mourn by writing down what the friendship gave her, and later stayed open to Tanu without comparing her to Pallavi.

qa.q: How might Tanu experience Manjula saying yes to the pottery class?
qa.a: Tanu probably felt glad and welcomed, laughing freely with Manjula at the second class.

grounding: The story shows a young woman grieving a friendship that ended without a fight, who lets herself mourn and remember it and stays open to a new friend.

Ishita, you're sad about Ankita and you think it's silly because you never fought. It's not silly. Let your Reena maasi tell you about Chitra.

We were inseparable at twenty. Same college bus, same library table, same terrible poetry. Then she married and moved to Jaipur, I started teaching in Indore, and the letters slowed down, then stopped. No quarrel. Nothing to forgive.

For a year I felt a strange ache. People asked about my husband, my job. Nobody asked about Chitra. It felt odd to be grieving someone who was still alive.

One evening I sat with her old letters and read them all. I cried. I thanked her in my head for teaching me to love poems.

That was the turning point. After that, when a new teacher, Farida, invited me to her home, I went. I didn't expect her to be Chitra. She became my own kind of friend.

qa.q: Where did Chitra move after she married?
qa.a: She moved to Jaipur.

qa.q: What did young Reena feel for that year after the letters stopped?
qa.a: She felt a strange, lonely ache of grief for a friend who was still alive.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena's story?
qa.a: Reading Chitra's old letters and letting herself cry and feel grateful, which freed her to accept Farida's friendship without comparing.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Reena when she accepted the invitation?
qa.a: Farida likely saw a warm new colleague willing to be her friend, without knowing about the loss behind it.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman grieving a friendship that faded without a fight, who mourns it and stays open to new friends without comparing.
